text:
Chapter Thirty-One


Since she had proposed a day at the beach, Arthur had been imagining what Maggie would look like in her bathing suit. When she tumbled out of her car onto the asphalt, already hot with the early summer sun, she was unfortunately covered, wearing a long, gauzy dress that only hinted at what was underneath. She had on a floppy sun hat and round sunglasses, carrying another one of her Diadhan conference tote bags with a brightly colored towel sticking out of it.


“Do you feel this, Dahlia?” Maggie shouted as Dahlia joined her. “The temperature is above sixty-five. The sun is actually shining. Gods above, I can finally defrost.” She was practically singing, and when she walked over to Arthur, there was a skip in her step he’d never seen before. He had expected her to be hesitant, tentative with her affection in front of Dahlia, but instead she fell into his arms. He held her to him, breathing in the way her shampoo mingled with the coconut sunscreen she’d covered herself in, and she wrapped her arms around his neck.


“I’m so glad you’re here,” he whispered. “I missed you.” He knew that sounded ridiculous. They had only been apart for half a day and one night, but that was long enough for her absence to feel like an ache.


“I missed you, too.”


When she’d gone to fortify the wards alone, he’d been so afraid that she was preparing to pull away, but that afternoon she had returned to their office and pushed him onto the couch, kissing him as if she’d been gone for days. She had practically dragged him back to her apartment without another word about needing space. He had stayed with her almost every night since, only driving out to Atlantia to gather clothing and grab the occasional coffee with Rory, who looked at him with sidelong glances like he had something to say. Yesterday afternoon, he’d returned to Atlantia for the night, to help Simon get ready for his baseball game today, which mostly involved a lot of talking through nerves and planning for the postgame ice cream cone they were going to eat.


“He’s wearing a bathing suit,” Dahlia said as they walked down the path that snaked through the dunes. “You owe me a coffee.”


Arthur glanced down at his outfit—old board shorts of Rory’s that were too short and the same Dartwood T-shirt he’d worn on their hike. “What did you think I was going to be wearing?”


“The last time we were on this beach, you were wearing a tweed jacket,” Maggie reminded him. “I wasn’t sure what you’d have on today.”


“It was cold!” When they reached the peak of the dune, he could see up and down the shore. It was still early, so the beach was empty except for people going for runs and walking their dogs. The glittering skyline of Atlantia was in the distance just across the cove and inlet north of the beach, with all of its peaking spires and shining windows.


Rory waved from the blanket and umbrella they’d arrived early to set up, walking up to meet them. He held out a hand to Dahlia. The night before, when Arthur had been trying to soothe Simon’s worries, he’d also been trying to ease his own. He was afraid he was making a mistake, bringing Maggie here to meet his brother and nephew. His father. Lane. Even with Dahlia here…But it was too late. He had reasoned with himself that even when the summer was over, he still hoped to have Maggie as a friend. Friends could meet his family. Right?


Then Rory was grasping Maggie’s hand in his, and Arthur’s worlds were colliding. “You must be Dahlia and Maggie. I’ve heard so much about you.”


“All good, I hope,” Maggie said as she dropped her stuff down on the blanket and kicked off her sandals. “I’ve heard a lot about you, too.”


Rory laughed, taking the beach chair Dahlia was carrying and setting it up beside his own chair, a detail that didn’t escape Arthur. “Let me guess, did he tell you some sob story about how I make too much fun of him?”


“Something like that,” she said with a grin. Arthur was stunned out of his worried thought spiral when Maggie tossed her sun hat onto the blanket and began tugging her sundress up over her head. Each inch it rose revealed another wondrous inch of Maggie and then a bathing suit that made Arthur forget he had been thinking about anything else at all. It crisscrossed her body with peeks of skin at her hip, her waist, between her breasts.


He knew he was staring, but he couldn’t help it. He wanted to walk over to the towel and lick the salty sweat off the stretches of skin the bathing suit revealed. When he finally tore his gaze away from her breasts, Maggie looked at him with a gleam in her eye, like she knew exactly what he was thinking, and it was what she’d wanted all along.


“Come sit over here, Dahlia,” Rory called, patting the chair he’d set up next to him. “Those two need some space.” He rolled his eyes and Dahlia laughed.


The two of them were already chatting like old friends by the time she sat down, and, after a moment, Dahlia stage-whispered to Maggie, “I guess prickliness doesn’t run in the family. Maybe you picked the wrong brother.”


“Thanks, Dahlia,” Arthur grumbled, stretching out on the blanket next to Maggie.


Maggie was still sitting, looking out toward the ocean with her elbows on her knees. “Where’s Simon?” she asked.


“My dad took him out fishing,” Arthur explained. “He was too anxious to sit around and wait for the game. Poor guy. We’ll meet them at the field.”


Maggie lay down beside him on the blanket, rolling over onto her stomach. Arthur had to practically sit on his hands to stop from running his fingers over the generous curve of her ass, right at the line her bathing suit cut. Maggie reached into her bag and pulled out two books—the romance and the fantasy novel they had been reading in her office. “You didn’t get to finish,” she explained, and soon she was lost in her book, distractedly playing with her bottom lip as she read.


Though Arthur opened the book, he couldn’t make himself focus on the words. Beside them with their chairs turned to look out at the horizon, Rory and Dahlia were swapping stories, each one more and more outlandish. Dahlia had just finished telling Rory about how she’d once crashed an ambassador’s dinner party after going on a date with her daughter, and Rory was telling a truly horrifying story about a run-in he’d had with a siren at work. Arthur recognized something in Rory’s wry grin, in the way he couldn’t stop tapping his finger on his beach chair as they talked, in the way he was spinning his stories so they were brighter, funnier than other times Arthur had heard them. He didn’t know Dahlia well, but she was leaning in, tossing her head back to laugh as his brother spoke. Interesting.


The sound of the ocean waves reminded him of Beltane, constant and sure, like a heartbeat. Maggie’s hand that had been playing with her lip was now in his hair, her nails swirling against his scalp in small circles, sending shivers down his neck. He leaned into her touch, and she smiled down at him from where she was propped up on her elbows, all without looking away from her book. This far from the pall, from Hawthorn, it was easier to glimpse the life he had agreed to give up at summer’s end. The quiet contentment and easy affection. He knew he shouldn’t want it, not after Maggie had made herself so clear, but he did. Gods below, he did.



—


Even as her cheeks turned pink and her hair started curling from the sweat, Maggie wasn’t sick of the heat. Her hand was out the window so the breeze could flow through her fingers as she and Arthur drove toward Simon’s favorite restaurant after his baseball game. She felt an almost dizzying contentment as Arthur sang along, badly, to a song on the radio, and she laughed more than she had in months.


The baseball game had been even more fun than she expected. When they arrived, Arthur had introduced her and Dahlia to Barry and Lane as colleagues and friends, and Maggie had felt the tension in her shoulders unwind. They ate buttery popcorn and hot dogs slathered in mustard, cheered loudly when Simon walked onto first base and then scored after his teammate hit a home run, and it was over before she knew it.


Maggie had originally planned to leave with Dahlia after the game, since her friend needed to get back to finish her summer course prep. It had been the perfect excuse to avoid an awkward dinner, but, at the last minute, she changed her mind and decided to go to dinner with Arthur and his family, even without the buffer of her best friend. Arthur’s face lit up when she suggested it, and she felt a thrill twisted with guilt, but she buried it as they drove to the restaurant.


Oyster Bay was down a long, winding road that came to a dead end at the marshy entrance to the water. It was an old restaurant, half on stilts over the marshland, and it had flooded in more than one big storm over the decades. The walls were wood paneled, the floors were uneven, and the ceilings were low. It was a little bit like stepping back in time, and Maggie thought it was such an interesting choice for a five-year-old’s favorite restaurant.


“My dad’s been coming here since he was a kid,” Arthur explained. “He’s been running an excellent PR campaign for the place since Simon was a baby.”


After Arthur parked the truck and they walked over the crushed oystershell gravel to the entrance, Maggie’s instinct was to close the gap between them and lace her fingers with Arthur’s. But when she thought about Barry or Lane or, worse, Simon, seeing them, she came to her senses. Even if there was a part of her that wanted to walk into that restaurant on his arm so there was no doubt who he was to her, the rational side of her won over and she kept her hands by her sides, tangled in the gauzy fabric of her sundress.


Inside, Arthur jogged over to the table that Rory and Simon had already commandeered as they waited for the rest of the family to arrive. Arthur picked up his nephew, swinging him around, and then squatted to talk to him about the baseball game since there hadn’t been time to debrief at the field. Maggie walked over slowly, unsure where she should sit, until Rory waved her over.


Even though she hadn’t had much of a chance to talk to Rory on her own, since Dahlia had seemed to occupy all of his time at the beach and he’d been on the sidelines during the baseball game, she had learned quickly that everything Arthur had told her about Rory was true. He somehow made her feel less awkward and more at ease just by inviting her over. “That was a great game,” she said as she sat down.


“Well, we certainly did finish the season. Nothing like watching twenty five-year-olds try to accomplish something together on the hottest day of the year.”


Maggie watched Arthur with Simon at the other end of the table. Somehow, their conversation about the baseball game had devolved completely into one about robots that both uncle and nephew were participating in enthusiastically. Suddenly, Rory stood up, waving toward the front of the restaurant as Barry and Lane walked over, positively beaming when they saw Arthur and Simon hunched together.


“Baseball star!” shouted Barry, doing a goofy little walk over to his grandson as he pretended to swing a bat. “Artie, wasn’t that game incredible? I couldn’t believe it when he hit that ball over the back fence.”


“Pop, we were all at the game. Don’t fib,” Rory admonished.


“Fine, he hit it straight toward the back fence, but it could have gone over. It definitely could have,” he finished, tousling Simon’s hair as the boy beamed up at his grandfather.


As everyone chose seats around the table, Simon plopped down in the chair next to her. Rory leaned over to him and said, “Hey, bud, let Uncle Artie sit there.”


Maggie waved him off. “Oh, no, it’s okay. I want to talk to him about the game.” She turned to Simon. “I saw you score!” He preened and she smiled as she asked, “What was your favorite part of the day?”


Simon considered this, his cute button nose a little red from the sun. “It was definitely the ice cream I got after.”


Maggie laughed. “You know, snacks are my favorite part of any baseball game, too.”


“Uncle Artie said if I’m good at dinner, he’ll get me another bowl.”


“Oh, well then, we’d better sit up straight and put our napkins on our laps. Do you think your uncle Artie will let me have some ice cream, too?”


Simon nodded seriously. “ ’Course he would.” They shook out their napkins, laying them primly on their laps.


When Maggie looked up, she saw Arthur at the other end of the table, watching her with Simon. “Thank you,” he said, and she shrugged, helping Simon set up a tic-tac-toe game on his menu.


Eventually they ordered their food, nostalgic fish fry platters and steaming bowls of soup, and the table settled into easy, overlapping conversation that Maggie had really only ever dreamed of for her own family. It was such a pleasant night. The restaurant windows were open, letting in a summer breeze, her skin was still warm from her hours in the sun, and the pall and all they still had to do to dissipate it felt miles and miles away.


She was showing Simon how to fold his napkin into a fortune teller when Barry asked, “So, Maggie, you’ve been sharing an office with our Artie?” She nodded and Barry let out a low whistle. “Hope he’s treating you right. Rory knows how tricky he is to get along with in close quarters.”


Rory rolled his eyes, and Arthur let out a grumbled, “Dad.” Then he explained, “Rory and I shared a bedroom one summer when Dad was renovating the bungalow. It was a nightmare.”


“You snore,” Rory shouted.


“You smell!” It was clearly an argument they’d had for many, many years.


Barry laughed, a soft expression in his eyes as he watched his sons bicker. Arthur was saying something like, “I can’t believe we’re talking about this now,” when Barry turned back to Maggie.


“But has he? Treated you right?”


Maggie flushed, though she hoped Barry couldn’t see it in the dim light of the restaurant. Beside him, Lane watched her with a small smile on her face, and Maggie stumbled over her words as she said, “He’s been wonderful. I’ll miss him when he goes back to the third floor.” She hadn’t meant anything by it, not really. It was the truth, after all. Her office would feel cavernous and quiet without him. But if she hadn’t meant anything by it, why did she suddenly feel like she was going to cry?


Finally, when they had cleared their plates and Maggie and Simon had finished their celebratory bowls of ice cream, Barry and Arthur fought over the check, but Arthur won by paying while Barry was in the bathroom.


As they walked back to their cars, Lane came up behind Maggie and put her hand on the younger woman’s shoulder. “I wanted to make sure I got a few words in before you left. These boys sure do love to talk.” It was a half-hearted sort of complaint, one she’d probably been making for all of their lives.


Maggie’s voice was conspiratorial as she said, “Arthur certainly does.”


Lane laughed lightly and then smiled at Maggie, tilting her head and considering her. “There’s been such a lightness to Arthur ever since you came into his life.” Maggie’s stomach twisted. What did she mean? “He’s had a hard time, these past few years.”


“I know,” Maggie said, her throat dry. A hard year that she was going to make harder. She felt shame curl in her gut. It didn’t matter how clear she had been when they started sleeping together, it was all muddy now. She may not have known when she kissed him in that tent how much he liked her, but she’d certainly realized it in the weeks since. It was in every touch, every time he whispered her name with reverence and awe.


Behind Lane, Rory and Arthur were swinging Simon back and forth, back and forth, between them, his little feet catching oyster shells with every swing until he was giggling. Oh gods, this was a mistake. She was going to break him, and the longer this went on, the worse it would be.


If Lane could see the panicked spiral of her thoughts, she didn’t show it. She just gave Maggie’s shoulder another squeeze. “Try not to break his heart too hard,” Lane finally said, walking over to Barry’s outstretched hand and getting into the car with one last glance back at Maggie.

facts.fact: 海滩解冻：65°F 以上终于能 defrost；她扑进他怀里不避 Dahlia——hesitancy 预期落空。
facts.anchor: Gods above, I can finally defrost.

facts.fact: 衣服梗：上次来这片海滩你还穿 tweed；他喊 It was cold——旧日拘谨变今日笑话。
世界相撞：Rory 握住她的手——他的两个世界相撞；Rory×Dahlia 聊成一片（摆椅子细节）。
泳装时刻：crisscross 缠身处处露肤；他看直眼想舔盐汗——她眼里有光：正合她意。
沙发阅读：海浪声如心跳（Beltane 同款）；她指腹绕他头皮画圈——他不该要这人生，Gods below, he did。
facts.anchor: constant and sure, like a heartbeat

facts.fact: 棒球赛：介绍 Barry/Lane 为同事与朋友；黄油爆米花芥末热狗；Simon 上垒得分全场欢呼。
与 Simon 的外交：她挥退 Rory 坐进 Uncle Artie 的位子——聊比赛/冰淇淋/铺餐巾坐直；他在桌那头说 Thank you。
facts.anchor: I want to talk to him about the game.

facts.fact: Barry 二次追问：可他到底待你好吗——她答他很好，他回三楼时我会想念他；话出口忽然想哭。
facts.anchor: But has he? Treated you right?

facts.fact: Lane 临别：Arthur 身上有了从未有的 lightness——自从你走进他的生活；Try not to break his heart too hard。
facts.anchor: Try not to break his heart too hard
